claim: eIF4E is a eukaryotic translation initiation factor that acts as an oncoprotein.
source: The eukaryotic translation initiation factor eIF4E, an oncoprotein, drives HA biosynthesis.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a characterization of eIF4E

claim: eIF4E stimulates production of enzymes that synthesize UDP-Glucuronic acid and UDP-N-Acetyl-Glucosamine, the building blocks of HA.
source: eIF4E stimulates production of enzymes that synthesize the building blocks of HA, UDP-Glucuronic acid and UDP-N-Acetyl-Glucosamine, as well as hyaluronic acid synthase which forms the disaccharide chain.
evidence: Supported by RIP experiments, mRNA export assays, and Western blots showing increased enzyme levels

claim: eIF4E stimulates production of hyaluronic acid synthase which forms the HA disaccharide chain.
source: eIF4E stimulates production of enzymes that synthesize the building blocks of HA, UDP-Glucuronic acid and UDP-N-Acetyl-Glucosamine, as well as hyaluronic acid synthase which forms the disaccharide chain.
evidence: Supported by RIP experiments showing HAS3 binding to eIF4E and Western blots showing increased HAS3 protein levels

claim: eIF4E inhibition alone repressed HA levels as effectively as directly targeting HA with hyaluronidase.
source: Strikingly, eIF4E inhibition alone repressed HA levels as effectively as directly targeting HA with hyaluronidase.
evidence: Supported by FACE analysis and confocal microscopy showing similar HA reduction with eIF4E knockdown/ribavirin treatment and HAse treatment

claim: HA was retained on the surface of high-eIF4E cells rather than being extruded into the extracellular space.
source: Unusually, HA was retained on the surface of high-eIF4E cells, rather than being extruded into the extracellular space.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing HA coating cell surfaces and forming protrusions

claim: Surface-associated HA was required for eIF4E's oncogenic activities.
source: Surface-associated HA was required for eIF4E's oncogenic activities suggesting that eIF4E potentiates an oncogenic HA program.
evidence: Supported by invasion and migration assays showing reduced oncogenic activity upon HAS3 knockdown or HAse treatment

claim: HA is a major component of the tumor microenvironment.
source: The microenvironment provides a functional substratum supporting tumour growth. Hyaluronan (HA) is a major component of this structure.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: HA is composed of repeating disaccharide units of UDP-Glucuronic Acid and UDP-N-Acetyl Glucosamine.
source: HA is composed of repeating disaccharides units of UDP-Glucuronic Acid and UDP-N-Acetyl Glucosamine.
evidence: Stated as established biochemical knowledge

claim: HA is synthesized by hyaluronic acid synthases (HAS), which are single transmembrane proteins localized to the inner-face of the plasma membrane.
source: HA is synthesized by hyaluronic acid synthases (HAS), which are single transmembrane proteins localized to the inner-face of the plasma membrane (Kultti et al., 2006; Lenart et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: HA chain length can be associated with differential functions including regulation of various cellular processes such as embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, wound healing and inflammation.
source: HA chain length can be associated with differential functions including regulation of various cellular processes such as embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, wound healing and inflammation and when dysregulated can promote EMT, tumor growth, and invasion (Goncharova et al., 2012; Toole, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: When dysregulated, HA can promote EMT, tumor growth, and invasion.
source: HA chain length can be associated with differential functions including regulation of various cellular processes such as embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, wound healing and inflammation and when dysregulated can promote EMT, tumor growth, and invasion (Goncharova et al., 2012; Toole, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Shorter HA chains are primarily synthesized by HAS3.
source: Shorter chains are primarily synthesized by HAS3 (Itano et al., 1999; Spicer and McDonald, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Shorter forms of HA are often associated with malignant phenotypes.
source: These shorter forms of HA are often associated with malignant phenotypes (Slevin et al., 2007; Slevin et al., 2002; West et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Artificial overexpression of HAS enzymes causes increased tumor growth in mouse xenograft models of prostate, breast and colon carcinomas.
source: Artificial overexpression of HAS enzymes causes increased tumor growth in mouse xenograft models of prostate, breast and colon carcinomas while its knockdown reverses this phenotype (Kultti et al., 2006; Koistinen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Knockdown of HAS enzymes reverses the increased tumor growth phenotype.
source: Artificial overexpression of HAS enzymes causes increased tumor growth in mouse xenograft models of prostate, breast and colon carcinomas while its knockdown reverses this phenotype (Kultti et al., 2006; Koistinen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: HA is cleaved by hyaluronidases which have been suggested to act as tumor suppressors.
source: Further, HA is cleaved by hyaluronidases which have been suggested to act as tumor suppressors; whereby increased expression inhibits tumor growth in colon and breast xenografts (Bertrand et al., 2005; Junker et al., 2003; Sá et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Increased hyaluronidase expression inhibits tumor growth in colon and breast xenografts.
source: Further, HA is cleaved by hyaluronidases which have been suggested to act as tumor suppressors; whereby increased expression inhibits tumor growth in colon and breast xenografts (Bertrand et al., 2005; Junker et al., 2003; Sá et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Increased HA levels are correlated with formation of less dense matrices to facilitate invasion and promote angiogenesis.
source: Increased HA levels are correlated with formation of less dense matrices to facilitate invasion and promote angiogenesis.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: Elevated levels of HA in the stroma around tumors is associated with poor outcome.
source: Elevated levels of HA in the stroma around tumors is associated with poor outcome (Anttila et al., 2000; Auvinen et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: HA can coat the surface of tumor cells with HA-based protrusions radiating from the cell surface.
source: In addition to surrounding tumors in some cases, HA can coat the surface of tumor cells with HA-based protrusions radiating from the cell surface (Ropponen et al., 1998; Setälä et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Overexpression of HAS3 alone is sufficient to induce the formation of an HA coat with microvillus-like protrusions on the cell surface.
source: Indeed, overexpression of HAS3 alone is sufficient to induce the formation of an HA coat with microvillus-like protrusions on the cell surface.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: CD44 is found to co-localize with surface HA coats but is not required for HA coat formation.
source: The major HA receptor CD44 is found to co-localize with these surface HA coats but is not required for HA coat formation.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: The levels of mRNAs encoding the enzymes in the HA biosynthetic pathways are often poor predictors of HA production.
source: Indeed, the levels of mRNAs encoding the enzymes in the biosynthetic pathways are often poor predictors of HA production (Nykopp et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: In endometrial and ovarian carcinomas, mRNA levels of HAS enzymes do not predict elevated HA levels.
source: For instance in endometrial and ovarian carcinomas, mRNA levels of HAS enzymes do not predict elevated HA levels in these specimens (Nykopp et al., 2010; Nykopp et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: eIF4E is highly expressed in many cancers and this correlates with increased invasion, metastases and poor prognosis.
source: eIF4E is highly expressed in many cancers and this correlates with increased invasion, metastases and poor prognosis (Assouline et al., 2015; Culjkovic-Kraljacic and Borden, 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Pettersson et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: eIF4E targeting with ribavirin led to objective responses including remissions in some acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients in early-stage clinical trials.
source: In early-stage clinical trials, eIF4E targeting with ribavirin led to objective responses including remissions in some acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients (Assouline et al., 2009; Assouline et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior clinical trial literature

claim: In mouse models, eIF4E overexpression is sufficient to drive tumor formation.
source: In mouse models, eIF4E overexpression is sufficient to drive tumor formation (Kentsis et al., 2004; Lazaris-Karatzas et al., 1990; Lazaris-Karatzas and Sonenberg, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: eIF4E modulates expression of selected transcripts through its roles in nuclear mRNA export and translation.
source: At the biochemical level, eIF4E modulates expression of selected transcripts through its roles in nuclear mRNA export and translation.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about eIF4E function

claim: Both mRNA export and translation functions of eIF4E contribute to its oncogenic potential.
source: Both these functions contribute to its oncogenic potential (Culjkovic-Kraljacic and Borden, 2013; Carroll and Borden, 2013; Osborne and Borden, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: In the cytoplasm, eIF4E binds all capped-RNAs regardless of whether it increases their translation efficiency.
source: In the cytoplasm, eIF4E binds all capped-RNAs regardless of whether it increases their translation efficiency (Rousseau et al., 1996; Culjkovic-Kraljacic et al., 2016; Graff and Zimmer, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: In the nucleus, eIF4E binds transcripts that are functional export targets.
source: However, in the nucleus, eIF4E binds transcripts that are functional export targets (Culjkovic et al., 2005; Culjkovic et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: eIF4E export target mRNAs typically contain a structurally-defined 50-nucleotide element known as an eIF4E sensitivity element (4ESE) in their 3' UTR and are m7G capped.
source: These export target mRNAs typically contain a structurally-defined 50-nucleotide element known as an eIF4E sensitivity element (4ESE) in their 3' UTR and are m7G capped (Culjkovic et al., 2006, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The 4ESE element is directly bound by the leucine-rich pentatricopeptide repeat (LRPPRC) protein which also directly binds the dorsal surface of eIF4E.
source: This element is directly bound by the leucine-rich pentatricopeptide repeat (LRPPRC) protein which also directly binds the dorsal surface of eIF4E.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the eIF4E export mechanism

claim: The eIF4E-4ESE RNA-LRPPRC complex binds the CRM1 nuclear pore receptor which transits it to the cytoplasm.
source: The eIF4E-4ESE RNA-LRPPRC complex in turn binds the CRM1 nuclear pore receptor which transits it to the cytoplasm (Topisirovic et al., 2009; Volpon et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: About 3500 RNAs have been shown to immunoprecipitate with eIF4E from the nuclear fraction of lymphoma cells.
source: To date, about 3500 RNAs have been shown to immunoprecipitate with eIF4E from the nuclear fraction of lymphoma cells suggesting that this is a broadly used mRNA export pathway (Culjkovic-Kraljacic et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: The transcript encoding hyaluronan synthase 3 (HAS3) binds eIF4E in nuclear RIPs with 2.6 fold enrichment.
source: These target mRNAs include hyaluronan synthase 3 (HAS3; 2.6 fold), as well as many of the enzymes involved in generating the UDP-Glucuronic acid and UDP-N-Acetyl Glucosamine precursors including hexokinase 1 (HK, ~15 fold), and phosphoglucomutase (PGM5, ~11 fold), amongst others (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from nuclear eIF4E RIP experiments shown in Figure 1b

claim: The transcript encoding hexokinase 1 (HK) binds eIF4E in nuclear RIPs with approximately 15 fold enrichment.
source: These target mRNAs include hyaluronan synthase 3 (HAS3; 2.6 fold), as well as many of the enzymes involved in generating the UDP-Glucuronic acid and UDP-N-Acetyl Glucosamine precursors including hexokinase 1 (HK, ~15 fold), and phosphoglucomutase (PGM5, ~11 fold), amongst others (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from nuclear eIF4E RIP experiments shown in Figure 1b

claim: The transcript encoding phosphoglucomutase (PGM5) binds eIF4E in nuclear RIPs with approximately 11 fold enrichment.
source: These target mRNAs include hyaluronan synthase 3 (HAS3; 2.6 fold), as well as many of the enzymes involved in generating the UDP-Glucuronic acid and UDP-N-Acetyl Glucosamine precursors including hexokinase 1 (HK, ~15 fold), and phosphoglucomutase (PGM5, ~11 fold), amongst others (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from nuclear eIF4E RIP experiments shown in Figure 1b

claim: The transcript encoding CD44 binds eIF4E in nuclear RIPs.
source: In addition to the HA biosynthetic machinery, other eIF4E targets identified in our RIP and fractionation studies included downstream effectors of HA for example CD44 as well as its signaling partners for example Ezrin and MMP9 (Figure 1b and c) (Montgomery et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from nuclear eIF4E RIP experiments shown in Figure 1b

claim: The transcript encoding Ezrin binds eIF4E in nuclear RIPs.
source: In addition to the HA biosynthetic machinery, other eIF4E targets identified in our RIP and fractionation studies included downstream effectors of HA for example CD44 as well as its signaling partners for example Ezrin and MMP9 (Figure 1b and c) (Montgomery et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from nuclear eIF4E RIP experiments shown in Figure 1b

claim: The transcript encoding MMP9 binds eIF4E in nuclear RIPs.
source: In addition to the HA biosynthetic machinery, other eIF4E targets identified in our RIP and fractionation studies included downstream effectors of HA for example CD44 as well as its signaling partners for example Ezrin and MMP9 (Figure 1b and c) (Montgomery et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from nuclear eIF4E RIP experiments shown in Figure 1b

claim: eIF4E overexpression increased mRNA export of HA biosynthetic enzyme transcripts two- to eight-fold relative to vector controls.
source: Nuclear mRNA export assays indicated that these mRNA-eIF4E interactions were functional since we observed increased mRNA export two- to eight-fold upon eIF4E overexpression relative to vector controls depending on the transcript monitored (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation experiments shown in Figure 1c

claim: The S53A eIF4E mutant did not promote export of HA biosynthetic enzyme mRNAs.
source: As expected, the S53A eIF4E mutant did not promote export of any of these mRNAs (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation experiments shown in Figure 1c

claim: The S53A eIF4E mutant is deficient in mRNA export and transformation but active in translation.
source: For comparison, we used the S53A eIF4E mutant which is deficient in mRNA export and transformation but active in translation (Osborne and Borden, 2015; Culjkovic-Kraljacic et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Total levels for HA biosynthetic enzyme target mRNAs were not affected by eIF4E overexpression.
source: Total levels for target mRNAs were not affected by eIF4E overexpression confirming that these effects were post-transcriptional (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: Most HA pathway transcripts do not appear to be substantially shifted on polysomes in U2Os cells.
source: We did not observe substantial shifts for most of these mRNAs on the polysomes with modest shifts to heavier polysomes including CD44, UAP, UGDH and UGP2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: Supported by polysomal profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b

claim: CD44, UAP, UGDH and UGP2 mRNAs showed modest shifts to heavier polysomes in eIF4E-overexpressing U2Os cells.
source: We did not observe substantial shifts for most of these mRNAs on the polysomes with modest shifts to heavier polysomes including CD44, UAP, UGDH and UGP2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: Supported by polysomal profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b

claim: c-Myc mRNA showed a substantial polysomal shift in eIF4E-overexpressing cells.
source: c-Myc mRNA, an established translational target of eIF4E, showed a substantial polysomal shift (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b) (Culjkovic-Kraljacic et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by polysomal profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b

claim: eIF4E overexpression led to increased protein levels of HAS3, HK, GFPT1, GNPNAT1, UAP1, UGDH, CD44 and Ezrin relative to vector controls.
source: Consistent with our above findings, eIF4E overexpression led to increased protein levels of the relevant enzymes, including HAS3, HK, GFPT1, GNPNAT1, UAP1, UGDH, as well as downstream effectors of HA function such as CD44 and Ezrin, relative to vector controls (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1d

claim: HA levels were substantially elevated in eIF4E overexpressing cells relative to vector controls or S53A eIF4E cells.
source: HA levels were substantially elevated in eIF4E overexpressing cells relative to vector controls or S53A eIF4E cells Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2a

claim: HA coated the cell surface and formed short, filamentous protrusions radiating from the surface coat in eIF4E overexpressing cells.
source: Strikingly, HA was not extruded into the media, but rather coated the cell surface and formed short, filamentous protrusions radiating from the surface coat in the eIF4E overexpressing cells (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2a,b

claim: Enzymatic depletion of HA with Streptomyces hyaluronidase virtually eliminated the HA signal.
source: Enzymatic depletion of HA with Streptomyces hyaluronidase (HAse) virtually eliminated the HA signal indicating that the staining was specific and suggesting that the structures were HA-dependent (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2a

claim: FACE analysis showed a ~ threefold increase in HA levels in eIF4E-overexpressing cells relative to vector controls.
source: We observe a ~ threefold increase in HA levels in eIF4E-overexpressing cells relative to vector controls.
evidence: Supported by FACE quantification data shown in Figure 2c

claim: HA levels in S53A-eIF4E cells were much lower than eIF4E overexpressing cells, and only modestly elevated relative to vector controls.
source: HA levels in S53A-eIF4E cells were much lower than eIF4E overexpressing cells, and only modestly elevated relative to vector controls consistent with the mutant's modest effects on the HA biosynthetic enzymes.
evidence: Supported by FACE quantification data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Removal of extracellular glucose led to reduction of HA signalling.
source: Further, removal of extracellular glucose led to reduction of HA signalling consistent with the use of glucose as the major metabolic precursor in this pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g–h).
evidence: Supported by glucose measurement and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g–h

claim: RNAi knockdown of eIF4E reduced HA to background levels.
source: We observed a reduction in HA to background levels via confocal microscopy using either ribavirin treatment or RNAi knockdown of eIF4E.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2d

claim: Ribavirin treatment reduced HA to background levels.
source: We observed a reduction in HA to background levels via confocal microscopy using either ribavirin treatment or RNAi knockdown of eIF4E.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2d

claim: FACE analysis showed a ~ ninefold reduction in HA levels for eIF4E knockdown relative to control RNAi.
source: Using FACE, we similarly observed a ~ ninefold reduction in HA levels for both eIF4E knockdown relative to control RNAi and ~2.5-fold for ribavirin treated versus untreated cells (Figure 2c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by FACE quantification data shown in Figure 2c

claim: FACE analysis showed a ~2.5-fold reduction in HA levels for ribavirin treated versus untreated cells.
source: Using FACE, we similarly observed a ~ ninefold reduction in HA levels for both eIF4E knockdown relative to control RNAi and ~2.5-fold for ribavirin treated versus untreated cells (Figure 2c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by FACE quantification data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Ribavirin directly binds eIF4E and inhibits its mRNA export and translation functions.
source: Ribavirin directly binds eIF4E and inhibits its mRNA export and translation functions (Pettersson et al., 2015; Kentsis et al., 2004; Volpon et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: MM6 AML cell line is characterized by elevated nuclear eIF4E levels.
source: First, we examined the MM6 AML cell line which is characterized by elevated nuclear eIF4E levels, and thus with increased mRNA export activity for eIF4E targets (Figure 3a–e and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3

claim: All mRNAs for the HA biosynthesis machinery including HAS3 and CD44 are eIF4E export targets in MM6 cells.
source: Using nuclear RIPs and mRNA export assays, we found that all mRNAs for the HA biosynthesis machinery including HAS3 and CD44 are eIF4E export targets in this cell type (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: Supported by RIP and export assay data shown in Figure 3a–c

claim: Transcripts encoding GPI are eIF4E export targets in MM6 cells.
source: These targets included transcripts encoding GPI, which was not an export target in U2Os cells.
evidence: Supported by export assay data shown in Figure 3b

claim: Transcripts encoding PGM5 were not well expressed in MM6 cells.
source: For instance, transcripts encoding PGM5 which were eIF4E targets in U2Os cells, were not well expressed in MM6 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of enzyme family members between cell types

claim: eIF4E bound to and exported PGM1 mRNAs in MM6 cells.
source: Instead, eIF4E bound to and exported PGM1 mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by RIP and export assay data in MM6 cells

claim: The surface of MM6 cells was characterized by HA coats.
source: Similar to U2Os cells, the surface of MM6 cells was characterized by HA coats.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 3d

claim: Ribavirin treatment reduced the mRNA export of HA enzymes and CD44 from two- to ninefold in MM6 cells.
source: We also found in MM6 cells that eIF4E targeting with ribavirin reduced the mRNA export of the corresponding HA enzymes and CD44 from two- to ninefold depending on the mRNA monitored (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by export assay data shown in Figure 3b

claim: Ribavirin did not alter total mRNA levels in MM6 cells.
source: Ribavirin did not alter total mRNA levels consistent with this being a post-transcriptional effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c

claim: Ribavirin treatment dramatically lowered protein levels for HAS3, HK, UGDH and CD44 in MM6 cells.
source: Consistently, ribavirin treatment dramatically lowered protein levels for the representative members of the HA biosynthetic machinery examined: HAS3, HK, UGDH as well as CD44 (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3c

claim: HA staining was reduced to background levels by ribavirin or HAse treatment in MM6 cells.
source: HA staining was reduced to background levels by ribavirin or HAse treatment as observed by HABP staining and confocal microscopy (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 3d

claim: 9/9 high-eIF4E AML specimens had HA coats and protrusions with HA staining 4–10 fold higher than the five normal human CD34+ specimens.
source: Consistent with the MM6 cells, 9/9 high-eIF4E AML specimens had HA coats and protrusions with HA staining 4–10 fold higher than the five normal human CD34+ specimens which all showed low-level, presumbably background, HA staining similar to intensities observed in vector controls U2Os cells (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy quantification shown in Figure 3e–f

claim: All five normal human CD34+ specimens showed low-level, presumably background, HA staining similar to intensities observed in vector control U2Os cells.
source: Consistent with the MM6 cells, 9/9 high-eIF4E AML specimens had HA coats and protrusions with HA staining 4–10 fold higher than the five normal human CD34+ specimens which all showed low-level, presumbably background, HA staining similar to intensities observed in vector controls U2Os cells (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy quantification shown in Figure 3e–f

claim: The HA coat is specific to the malignant state and not a general feature of blood cells.
source: These findings suggest that the HA coat is specific to the malignant state and not a general feature of blood cells (Figure 3e–f).
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of HA staining between AML specimens and normal CD34+ cells

claim: 66cl4 breast cancer cells had highly elevated nuclear eIF4E.
source: Next, we examined another high-eIF4E context, the breast cancer cell line 66cl4. These cells had highly elevated nuclear eIF4E, and also had readily visible HA-surface coats and protrusions as observed by confocal microscopy (Figure 3g).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 3g

claim: 66cl4 cells had readily visible HA-surface coats and protrusions.
source: Next, we examined another high-eIF4E context, the breast cancer cell line 66cl4. These cells had highly elevated nuclear eIF4E, and also had readily visible HA-surface coats and protrusions as observed by confocal microscopy (Figure 3g).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 3g

claim: Ribavirin treatment reduced HAS3 and CD44 levels in 66cl4 cells relative to untreated controls.
source: Ribavirin treatment reduced HAS3 and CD44 levels relative to untreated controls as well as dramatically reduced HA levels (Figure 3g).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3g,h

claim: Ribavirin treatment dramatically reduced HA levels in 66cl4 cells.
source: Ribavirin treatment reduced HAS3 and CD44 levels relative to untreated controls as well as dramatically reduced HA levels (Figure 3g).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3g

claim: There could be active translation down the length of the protrusions in eIF4E-overexpressing and 66cl4 cells.
source: Furthermore, we observed by in situ translation studies using fluorescence non-canonical amino-acid tagging (FUNCAT), that there could be active translation down the length of the protrusions in eIF4E-overexpressing and 66cl4 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–b).
evidence: Supported by FUNCAT imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–b

claim: Translation foci in the protrusions are cyclohexamide dependent.
source: These translation foci are cyclohexamide dependent validating them as sites of ongoing translation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–b).
evidence: Supported by FUNCAT imaging data with cyclohexamide treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–b

claim: eIF4E-overexpressing cells invaded matrigel fourfold better than vector controls.
source: Starting with invasion, we observed that eIF4E-overexpressing cells invaded matrigel fourfold better than vector controls (Figure 4a,b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b and e–f).
evidence: Supported by matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 4a,b

claim: The S53A eIF4E mutant increased invasion by only 50% relative to vector controls.
source: By contrast, the S53A eIF4E mutant increased invasion by only 50% relative to vector controls consistent with its more modest effects on HA production by FACE (Figure 2c; Figure 4—figure supplement 1e–f and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e–f

claim: RNAi to eIF4E reduced invasion by ~2.5-fold in both eIF4E overexpressing and vector control cells.
source: In both eIF4E overexpressing and vector control cells, RNAi to eIF4E or ribavirin treatment reduced invasion by ~2.5-fold consistent with the significant reduction in HA levels (Figure 2c, Figure 4e–f and Figure 4—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: Supported by matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 4e–f

claim: Ribavirin treatment reduced invasion by ~2.5-fold in both eIF4E overexpressing and vector control cells.
source: In both eIF4E overexpressing and vector control cells, RNAi to eIF4E or ribavirin treatment reduced invasion by ~2.5-fold consistent with the significant reduction in HA levels (Figure 2c, Figure 4e–f and Figure 4—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: Supported by matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 4e–f

claim: RNAi to HAS3 reduced the invasion activity of eIF4E by ~ fivefold in eIF4E overexpressing cells.
source: We observed that RNAi to HAS3 reduced the invasion activity of eIF4E by ~ fivefold in eIF4E overexpressing cells (to levels of RNAi controls) and 2.5-fold in vector controls where the effects of endogenous eIF4E are likely being targeted.
evidence: Supported by matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 4a,b

claim: RNAi to HAS3 reduced invasion by 2.5-fold in vector controls.
source: We observed that RNAi to HAS3 reduced the invasion activity of eIF4E by ~ fivefold in eIF4E overexpressing cells (to levels of RNAi controls) and 2.5-fold in vector controls where the effects of endogenous eIF4E are likely being targeted.
evidence: Supported by matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 4a,b

claim: HAS3 knockdown did not affect eIF4E levels.
source: HAS3 knockdown did not affect eIF4E levels as observed by western blot (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4d

claim: RNAi to HAS3 decreased HA levels to background.
source: Furthermore, confocal microscopy experiments revealed that RNAi to HAS3 decreased HA levels to background consistent with its baseline invasion activity (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4c

claim: HAS3 knockdown lowered HA levels by ~ ninefold relative to RNAi controls by FACE.
source: FACE studies also revealed that HAS3 knockdown lowered HA levels by ~ ninefold relative to RNAi controls (Figure 2c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by FACE quantification data shown in Figure 2c

claim: HAse treatment reduced invasion by 40% relative to untreated controls.
source: We observed that HAse treatment reduced invasion by 40% relative to untreated controls.
evidence: Supported by matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 4e,f

claim: Ribavirin decreased invasion by 60% relative to untreated controls.
source: For comparison, ribavirin decreased invasion by 60% consistent with its reduction of HA to background levels.
evidence: Supported by matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 4e,f

claim: The combination of ribavirin and HAse reduced invasion by 80%.
source: Strikingly, the combination of ribavirin and HAse reduced invasion by 80% (Figure 4e–f and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: Supported by matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 4e–f

claim: The length of time between HAse treatment and re-emergence of HA in eIF4E-overexpressing cells was 12 hr.
source: Given the length of time between HAse treatment and re-emergence of HA in eIF4E-overexpressing cells was 12 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h), we treated cells with HAse every 8 hr to ensure HA was depleted during the course of the experiments.
evidence: Supported by time-course confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1h

claim: Increased migration was observed in eIF4E-overexpressing cells relative to vector controls.

claim: Knockdown of HAS3 reduced eIF4E-dependent migration by ~ fourfold.
source: Knockdown of HAS3 reduced eIF4E-dependent migration by ~ fourfold while treatment with HAse reduced it by almost twofold indicating this was also an HA dependent phenomenon.
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data shown in Figure 4g,h

claim: Treatment with HAse reduced eIF4E-dependent migration by almost twofold.
source: Knockdown of HAS3 reduced eIF4E-dependent migration by ~ fourfold while treatment with HAse reduced it by almost twofold indicating this was also an HA dependent phenomenon.
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data shown in Figure 4g,h

claim: Ribavirin treatment reduced metastasis by 3-fold in an eIF4E-dependent pulmonary metastatic mouse model using 66cl4 cells.

evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: A 50% decrease in HA levels was observed in the lungs of ribavirin-treated mice relative to controls.

claim: HA surrounded tumor cells in metastatic lung tissue.
source: HA surrounded tumor cells indicating that HA was adjacent to and/or on the surface of these cells.

claim: HA was also found in normal tissues, consistent with its major structural role in the microenvironment.
source: As expected, HA was also found in normal tissues, consistent with its major structural role in the microenvironment.

claim: eIF4E overexpression led to highly elevated CD44 protein levels.

claim: CD44 coated the cell surface in eIF4E-overexpressing cells.

claim: CD44 and HA co-localized on the cell surface.

claim: Inhibition of CD44 with RNAi reduced eIF4E-mediated invasion by ~ fourfold.

claim: CD44-blocking antibodies (mAb A3D8) reduced eIF4E-mediated invasion by ~ threefold.

claim: HA is essential for eIF4E-mediated invasion.

claim: CD44 and perhaps other co-factors are likely required for eIF4E-mediated invasion.
source: Thus, although HA is essential for eIF4E-mediated invasion, its co-factors CD44 and perhaps others, are likely also required for this activity.

claim: The HA coat and/or protrusions need to be armed with CD44 to support the invasion potential of eIF4E overexpressing cells.
source: This suggests that the HA coat and/or protrusions need to be armed with CD44 to support the invasion potential of eIF4E overexpressing cells.

claim: In high-eIF4E cells, HA is likely directly binding CD44 to activate signaling pathways in neighboring cells and/or in its own cells leading to autocrine stimulation.

claim: The entire HA-network is subjected to coordinated post-transcriptional control by eIF4E.
source: Our studies demonstrate that the entire HA-network is subjected to coordinated post-transcriptional control by eIF4E, in effect, an RNA regulon controlling HA biosynthesis and ultimately cell surface architecture.
evidence: Supported by the comprehensive data showing eIF4E controls multiple components of the HA pathway

claim: eIF4E controls an RNA regulon controlling HA biosynthesis and ultimately cell surface architecture.
source: Our studies demonstrate that the entire HA-network is subjected to coordinated post-transcriptional control by eIF4E, in effect, an RNA regulon controlling HA biosynthesis and ultimately cell surface architecture.
evidence: Inferred from the coordinated regulation of multiple HA pathway components by eIF4E

claim: HA levels would scale with both elevation and loss of control of eIF4E.
source: Our data suggest that HA levels would scale with both elevation and loss of control of eIF4E.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing HA levels correlate with eIF4E activity

claim: In normal cells with less eIF4E and tighter eIF4E regulation, HA biosynthesis would be expected to be lower.
source: Thus, in normal cells with less eIF4E and tighter eIF4E regulation, HA biosynthesis would be expected to be lower.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of HA levels between normal and cancer cells

claim: In cancer cells, elevation of eIF4E and loss of key regulators of eIF4E such as PRH/Hex in AML allows more HA pathway transcripts to be bound to eIF4E in the nucleus, have their export elevated and in some cases be better translated.
source: In cancer cells, elevation of eIF4E and loss of key regulators of eIF4E such as PRH/Hex in AML (Topisirovic et al., 2003a; Topisirovic et al., 2003b), allows more of these transcripts to be bound to eIF4E in the nucleus, have their export elevated and in some cases be better translated.
evidence: Inferred from the data and supported by citations about eIF4E regulation

claim: Factors that modulate the levels, localization, or phosphorylation of eIF4E are positioned to profoundly affect HA production and the global activity of the HA network.
source: For instance, factors that modulate the levels, localization, or phosphorylation of eIF4E are positioned to profoundly affect HA production and the global activity of the HA network.
evidence: Inferred from the demonstrated control of HA production by eIF4E

claim: Targeting eIF4E with RNAi knockdown or ribavirin treatment reduced HA levels as effectively as direct targeting with HAse.
source: Indeed, targeting eIF4E with RNAi knockdown or ribavirin treatment reduced HA levels as effectively as direct targeting with HAse.
evidence: Supported by FACE and confocal microscopy data comparing eIF4E inhibition to HAse treatment

claim: eIF4E drove the production of cell-associated HA which fundamentally modified the cell-surface architecture facilitating invasion and metastases.
source: We note that eIF4E drove the production of cell-associated HA which in turn, fundamentally modified the cell-surface architecture facilitating invasion and metastases.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy showing cell-surface HA and invasion/migration assays

claim: eIF4E may specifically drive an oncogenic HA-programme, in contrast to typical situations where this large glycosaminoglycan is extruded into the matrix.
source: Thus eIF4E may specifically drive an oncogenic HA-programme, in contrast to typical situations where this large glycosaminoglycan is extruded into the matrix.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HA is retained on cell surfaces in high-eIF4E cells rather than being extruded

claim: It is not yet known if the ability to modulate HA is a property unique to eIF4E, or if other oncoproteins initiate a similar programme.
source: It is not yet known if the ability to modulate HA is a property unique to eIF4E, or if other oncoproteins initiate a similar programme.
